newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistani police clash with Islamist protesters.
newsitem.headline: Pakistani police clash with Islamist protesters.

text.p: Pakistani police fired dozens of rounds of teargas at Islamic militants trying to reach the parliament building in Islamabad on Sunday, witnesses said.
The opposition Jamaat-i-Islami (JI) party had planned to bring a million supporters to the capital for a sit-in against alleged corruption under Prime Minister Benazir Bhutto's rule.
Witnesses said a few hundred JI activists hiding in the Aabpara market area had emerged suddenly on a main road that leads to parliament on the city's Constitution Avenue.
The demonstrators hurled stones at police, who responded with canisters spewing clouds of teargas. The JI activists picked up some of the canisters and threw them back.
No injuries were immediately reported in the clash, the first reported inside Islamabad city limits on Sunday.
Up to 10,000 JI supporters, some wearing headbands and carrying Korans, were halted at a police roadblock on the outskirts of the nearby city of Rawalpindi, witnesses said.
Gunfire erupted earlier near the town of Saray Alamgir, about 100 km (62 miles) southeast of Islamabad, after police intercepted JI vehicles heading for the capital.
The official APP news agency said three policemen and the driver of the assistant commissioner of Jehlum district in Punjab province had been wounded in that clash.
The shooting occurred at about 7.30 a.m. (0230 GMT) after police teargassed the Jamaat-i-Islami procession.
The cavalcade drove on, only to be intercepted about half an hour later further down the road. The protesters burst through the second barricade, pelting stones at police.
Security forces backed by armoured troop carriers and water cannons blocked Islamabad's access roads overnight with heavy containers, barbed wire and sandbagged posts.
In nearby Rawalpindi, JI militants wore headbands inscribed "There is no god but Allah" as organisers distributed nuts and what they said was holy water from Mecca in Saudi Arabia.
"Revolution, revolution, Islamic revolution," they chanted. "My wish, your wish, martyrdom, martyrdom."

Up to 10,000 protesters, led by JI chief Qazi Hussain Ahmad riding in an open truck, halted 200 metres (yards) from riot police manning a barricade of containers. Police fired 15 to 20 teargas canisters at a few activists who came too close.
Ahmad sent a delegation forward to try to negotiate free passage for the marchers, but there was no word on the outcome.
The JI leader on Saturday denounced Bhutto's government for attributing violent intentions to his followers. He said JI had never been lawless and urged his supporters to show restraint.
The government would be responsible for any "brutal use of force against peaceful protesters", he warned in a statement.
Paramilitary troops with truck-mounted machineguns guarded the parliament, as well as the prime minister's secretariat, president's palace, foreign ministry and diplomatic enclave.
The authorities diverted or cancelled 24 passenger trains on Saturday, re-routing inter-city services to avoid Rawalpindi.
All schools and universities stayed closed on Sunday and attendance at government offices was thin.

JI leaders said the security forces had rounded up more than 5,500 of its supporters to try to disrupt the protest. An Interior Ministry spokesman said the JI figure was exaggerated, but could not say how many people had been seized.
Interior Minister Naseerullah Babar on Thursday offered to free all JI detainees if the party agreed to shift its sit-in to Liaquat Bagh park in Rawalpindi. JI rejected the offer.
Three people were killed and 60 wounded when gunfire broke out during a JI demonstration in Rawalpindi in June.
Some newspaper commentators criticised JI, which won only three seats in parliament at the last election in 1993, for courting more bloodshed by going ahead with its protest.

"Qazi (Hussain Ahmad) is aware of the dangers and by persisting with his sit-in plans is deliberately provoking a confrontation that will produce nothing but dead bodies," said a commentator in the English-language daily The News.
